Sorry for the late reply, I had a very busy day.

The cause of the confusion isn't astronomical issue, but a cultural one. All celebrations referring to it are incredibly similar. Both St. Johns day and Midsummer use sun symbolism as in lighting fires or picking flowers (St. John's wort as the symbol for the sun, starting to bloom around that day!). It's obvious that the celebrations are closely related to the Summer Solstice and have their origin there, but both are celebrated on the 23rd/24th or generally on a date around the Solstice, but not necessarily on the Solstice itself.
It's similar to Christmas and the the Winter Solstice.

I'm a bit late to the party, but here it goes anyway:

We celebrated it on saturday. This year we used the story of Balder to symbolise the dying of the sun. When the sun is at it's highest we make a circle of stones, calling to the dwarves (nordri sudri austri vestri) as we place the stone. We walk to an ancient holy place, have a small blót on the past summer. When the sun is setting we stand in the circle and the leader of the ritual will tell the story of Balder in different parts. We take the sacrificial bread of Balder and everyone can stand in a cirle and throw stuff at it (knives, axes, you name it) and then one person is blindfolded and gets a bow and arrow. The arrow is dipped in mistletoe and Balder is shot by him (he is being guided) and the sun has set.

Then we make a huge pyre which is hollow from the inside. We place Balder and other sacrifices (personal sacrifices, blooming flowers etc) in the pyre. Then four people carry torches and stand at each of the stones (north, west etc) then the leader of the ritual speaks and calls forth the nine kinds of wood and the nine kinds of herbs to be placed as sacrifice on the pyre. One person makes a fire and the torches and pyre is set aflame. People jump over the fire for fertillity and such. We keep the ash to be put into the fire and sacrificial bread of the coming year, to emphasize the continuing cirle of summer and winter.

We also make a wheel from wood and blooming flowers that will dry for the coming half year and which will get spinned around and burned on the midwinter solstice.

There might be a threshold of being so impressed that a person is no longer afraid of the weapon firing at them. This tank gun might be at that threshold, and so it holds no fear factor. "It would be an honor to die to such weaponry," comes to mind.

Color me skeptical. It's easy to make a more powerful tank gun by simply scaling up the size. Unfortunately, a bigger gun will create serious engineering problems in making a tank that works. The Chinese will likely have to design completely new vehicles if they don't want their shiny new gun to destroy tank transmissions every time it fires.

A tank engineered to carry China's new 7.5 meter long gun will likely be bigger, heavier, and more expensive to build and maintain than the tanks fielded by everyone else. A marginally more powerful gun is likely a bad tradeoff for all the disadvantages that will come with it.

The only purpose I can see in building a vehicle around that is to serve as either a self propelled gun. Not nearly as armored as a tank, usually behind the main lines, firing indirectly at the enemy. Even then, the equipment needed to elevate that beast would probably be a seriously limiting factor.
